paper_metadata.title: Pricing multi-asset derivatives by variational quantum algorithms

summary: The paper proposes a variational quantum algorithm for pricing multi-asset derivatives by solving the finite-difference discretized Black-Scholes PDE with VQS and estimating the price via a SWAP-test overlap with a probability-distribution state. In numerical simulations for a single-asset double knock-out barrier option, the authors test 4-, 5-, and 6-qubit ansätze with 2 or 4 layers and report agreement with the analytical benchmark, with one stated price error of 1.2e-05 for the initial-state approximation study.

experiments.description: Variational quantum simulation of the discretized Black-Scholes PDE for pricing a multi-asset derivative, with the derivative price extracted via SWAP test against a probability-distribution state. Numerical validation is shown for a single-asset double knock-out barrier option using statevector-style simulation.

algorithm.variant: variational quantum simulation (VQS) for linear ODEs applied to the finite-difference discretized Black-Scholes PDE
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient layered ansatz with repeated CZ entanglement layers and RY rotations
algorithm.optimizer: Euler method for parameter evolution; L-BFGS-B used only in a separate initial-state approximation study
algorithm.parameter_initialization: VQS starts from parameters set so the ansatz is identity at tau=0; in the numerical example, initial state approximation is optimized with L-BFGS-B

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Grid points of the discretized asset-price domain are mapped to computational basis states |k>; one n-qubit register encodes N_gr = 2^n grid points
problem_formulation.objective_function: Price the derivative by solving the Black-Scholes PDE backward in time and compute V(0,s0) ≈ e^{-r t_ter} <p(t_ter)|V(t_ter)>
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Boundary conditions are incorporated through the inhomogeneous term C(t) in the discretized ODE; knock-out barriers set boundary values to zero

problem_instance.description: Multi-asset derivative pricing under the Black-Scholes model; numerical experiment focuses on a single-asset double knock-out barrier option

dataset_specification.benchmark_name: single-asset double barrier option analytical benchmark
dataset_specification.preprocessing: finite-difference discretization of asset price domain; analytical probability density used for p(t,s) in simulation

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Asset price interval [l,u] discretized into ngr grids; in the example l=0.5, u=2.0; no log-transform used
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare VQS-derived prices against analytical solution and classical finite-difference method; numerical simulations shown for 4, 5, and 6 qubits and 2 or 4 ansatz layers

hardware.framework: NumPy-based simulation; quantum-circuit simulation not tied to a named SDK
hardware.classical_solver: Euler method for ODE parameter evolution; L-BFGS-B for initial-state fitting in a separate demonstration

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct finite-difference matrices for the Black-Scholes PDE; prepare probability distribution state and payoff state analytically/variationally
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Take square root of SWAP-test overlap and discount by e^{-r t_ter} to estimate present price

results.unit: not explicitly reported; qualitative statement that larger qubit count and more layers improve agreement with analytical solution

classical_baselines.unit: not numerically stated; compared via figures for 16, 32, and 64 grid points

speedup_claims.factor: avoids the (1/epsilon)^{O(d)} bottleneck; measurement scaling O(1/epsilon^2 (log(1/epsilon))^d)
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical finite-difference method and conventional quantum algorithms
speedup_claims.conditions: under stated assumptions for the SWAP-test overlap bound and efficient state preparation
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper notes the overall complexity is heuristic due to variational quantum simulation; exponential dependence on number of assets d remains in the SWAP-test measurement bound, but not the (1/epsilon)^{O(d)} factor.

speedup_claims.factor: O(poly(d log(1/epsilon))) circuit complexity for VQS subroutines
speedup_claims.conditions: assuming efficient decomposition of operators and state preparation
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an asymptotic claim for circuit construction and VQS, not an empirical benchmark.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(poly(d log(1/ϵ))) for circuit construction and VQS subroutines; SWAP-test measurements scale as O(1/ϵ^2 (log(1/ϵ))^d) under stated assumptions
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical finite-difference method scales as O((1/ϵ)^{O(d)})

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; only toy-scale simulations with 4, 5, and 6 qubits and 16/32/64 grid points are reported.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Efficient state preparation for the probability distribution and payoff state, plus scalable VQS and SWAP-test overlap estimation; the paper assumes these are available but does not demonstrate them on hardware.
limiting_factors: No real quantum hardware results; simulations are NumPy-based.
The paper assumes efficient preparation of |p(t_ter)> and |V(0)> rather than demonstrating it.
SWAP-test measurement cost still scales exponentially in the number of assets d through (log(1/epsilon))^d.
Overall algorithmic complexity is heuristic because it relies on variational quantum simulation.

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper reports numerical simulations with NumPy and no real QPU or noisy backend.
Num_qubits is not given as a single fixed value for the experiment; the paper reports example simulations with 4, 5, and 6 qubits.
Circuit depth not explicitly reported as a total depth; only ansatz layer counts (2 and 4) are given, so depth is left null/inferred only at the layer level.
Speedup order is reported qualitatively as avoiding the (1/ϵ)^{O(d)} bottleneck; the paper claims O(1/ϵ^2 (log(1/ϵ))^d) measurement scaling under assumptions.
The paper presents a variational algorithm and numerical simulations only; it does not report a demonstrated quantum advantage over classical methods.
The reported scaling is theoretical, with no hardware benchmark or crossover point established.
